member_targets: The set of explicit demarcation criteria (specific tests, thresholds, or distinguishing properties) that would mark the point at which text-mediated competence and sensorimotor competence can no longer be told apart in an embodied language-model system.
The specific evaluative benchmarks or criteria that would mark the point at which the distinction between text-mediated competence and sensorimotor competence ceases to be meaningful.

The specific sensor suite, action channels, feedback timing, and control-architecture configuration that would be sufficient to fully eliminate (not merely blur) the distinction between text-mediated and sensorimotor competence.

The causal relationship between differences in embodiment configuration (sensor quality, action channels, feedback timing, control architecture) and the degree or nature of a language model's capacity for ongoing learning from the consequences of its own actions.
The set of explicit demarcation criteria that would separate text-mediated competence from sensorimotor competence in embodied language-model systems where that boundary is becoming indistinct.

The causal relationship between embodiment parameters (sensor fidelity and feedback latency/timing) and the magnitude and nature of behavioral/capability differences observed when the same language model is placed in different embodiments.

A comparative assessment of the relative magnitude and manner in which sensor feedback latency versus model architecture differences constrain a language model's capacity to learn from action-consequence feedback in an embodied loop.

A component-by-component account of the particular constraints each embodiment factor—sensor quality, action channels, and feedback timing—places on what a language model can practically do when embodied.

A comparative assessment identifying which control architecture designs best couple language-model outputs to real-time sensorimotor feedback loops, and the effectiveness criteria distinguishing them.

The causal effect of feedback characteristics (latency/timing and sensory modality/type) in a sensorimotor loop on a language model's capacity for learning and behavioral adaptation — i.e., a mechanism-level account of how varying feedback timing and nature changes adaptive performance.
The mechanisms by which feedback latency/timing and control architecture design shape the sensorimotor performance of a language model embedded in a perception-action loop.
The causal effect of sensor feedback latency (timing delay between action and perceived consequence) on a language-model-controlled embodied system's capacity for learning and behavioral adaptation.

The mechanism by which differences in embodiment configuration (sensor quality, action channels, feedback timing, control architecture) change a language model's capacity to detect and correct its own errors from consequences of its actions.

The causal effect of action-to-sensor-feedback delay on an embodied language-model system's capacity for learning and adaptation, i.e., the mechanism by which feedback timing shapes adaptive performance.

The causal mechanism by which specific embodiment parameters (sensor fidelity, feedback latency) produce divergent observed behavior in a fixed underlying language model across different physical setups.

The causal mechanism by which the latency/timing of sensorimotor feedback in an embodied loop shapes what a given language model can practically do, i.e., how variation in feedback timing changes the system's effective capabilities.

The mechanism by which control architecture mediates the conversion of sensor input into physical action in an embodied language-model system — i.e., which architectural features and processes govern effective sensorimotor translation.

The particular embodiment-level variables (e.g., sensor quality, action channels, feedback timing, control architecture, and any others) and how each shapes which practical capabilities a model exhibits in that system.
The specific causal mechanisms by which differences in sensor fidelity and feedback latency produce differing behavior in embodied systems built around the same underlying language model.

The set of embodiment-specific factors (e.g., sensor quality, action channels, feedback timing, control architecture) and their relative weight in determining how much a given embodiment expands or constrains a language model's practical capabilities.

An identification of which particular capabilities vary most across different embodiments (sensor, actuator, feedback, and control-architecture configurations) wrapping an identical underlying language model, ranked by magnitude of divergence.

An enumeration of concrete, observed capability differences exhibited by one and the same language model when placed in different embodiments (i.e., which specific practical abilities were seen to change with sensors, actuators, feedback timing, or control architecture).
The specific mechanisms by which a control architecture surrounding a language model enables or limits what that model can practically do when embodied.

The specific classes of embodied capability that arise exclusively above some threshold of sensorimotor feedback richness and speed, as distinct from capabilities present with sparse or slow feedback.

The causal relationship between sensorimotor feedback-loop properties (latency/timing and sensor-action fidelity) and whether an embodied language model acquires genuine understanding rather than surface pattern matching — i.e., what feedback characteristics produce which kind of competence.
The causal mechanism by which variation in sensor fidelity and feedback latency changes what an embodied language-model system can practically do.

A specification of concrete, reliable diagnostic criteria or benchmark tests that would discriminate text-mediated competence from genuine sensorimotor competence in embodied language-model systems, including what measurable behavioral signatures would mark the distinction as integration increases.

The relationship between sensorimotor coupling properties (sensor/actuator fidelity, feedback latency) and whether a system attains genuine understanding rather than surface input-output pattern matching — i.e., whether and how richer, faster embodiment produces a qualitative kind-change in competence rather than a quantitative improvement.
The specific causal mechanisms by which variation in sensor quality and feedback timing changes what a language-model-driven embodied system can actually accomplish in real-world tasks.

The causal mapping from specific embodiment parameters (sensor fidelity, feedback latency) to the particular behavioral differences they produce in an otherwise identical language model — i.e., which behaviors change and in what way as those parameters vary.

The causal mechanism by which sensor fidelity and the latency/timing of consequence feedback determine whether an embodied language model can acquire and use information about its actions' outcomes — i.e., how these embodiment parameters enable or impair consequence-based learning.

The effect of feedback latency/delay on a sensor-actuator-coupled language model system's capacity to associate actions with their consequences and adapt accordingly — i.e., the mechanism by which timing lags degrade (or alter) credit assignment, learning, and adaptive control.

The functional relationship by which embodiment properties—specifically sensor fidelity and feedback latency—produce differences in reliability and task performance across systems that share an identical underlying language model.

The set of concrete measurable criteria or benchmark tests (and their threshold values) that would mark the point at which a sensor-and-actuator-coupled language model's competence counts as sensorimotor rather than text-mediated.

The identity of specific control architecture designs that most effectively allow a language model to incorporate fast sensorimotor feedback loops, i.e., a comparative ranking or specification of architectural approaches for closed-loop embodied control.

The mechanism by which the latency/timing of sensory-action feedback loops shapes what an embodied language model can practically do, isolating timing's contribution among the other embodiment factors.

The criteria or decision rule for identifying the threshold point at which an embodied sensor-actuator system stops counting as an information-processing tool and counts as a genuinely autonomous agent.
The causal mechanism by which sensor feedback latency and fidelity shape a model's capacity for real-time behavioral learning and adaptation in an embodied loop.

The relative contribution (comparative weight) of embodiment factors — sensor/actuator hardware quality and control architecture — versus the underlying language model in determining an embodied agent's practical performance.

The causal mechanisms by which embodiment properties (sensor quality, action channels, feedback timing, control architecture) shape whether and how well a language-model-driven system can detect and correct its own errors through consequence feedback.

The causal effect of feedback latency on a sensorimotor-embodied language model's capacity to acquire and refine action-outcome learning — i.e., the mechanism by which delayed consequence signals degrade (or otherwise alter) credit assignment and learning from interaction.
A component-by-component account of how each embodiment factor — sensor quality, action channels, and feedback timing — specifically enhances or constrains system capability in practical deployments.
The causal mechanism by which the latency/timing of sensory feedback in an embodied control loop changes what practical capabilities the same language model can exhibit.

The causal effect of variation in embodiment components (sensor quality, action channels, feedback timing, control architecture) on what a given language model can practically do when embedded in such a system — i.e., the mechanism/pathways by which these system-level factors modulate practical capability.

The causal mechanism by which specific embodiment properties (sensor fidelity and feedback latency) alter what an unchanged language model can practically accomplish when embedded in a sensorimotor loop.

The specific types or categories of embodied capability that arise once sensorimotor coupling passes sufficient richness and speed — i.e., what qualitatively new competences appear, not whether or when a threshold is crossed.

The identity of specific control architecture designs that are most effective at enabling a language model to learn from rapid multimodal sensorimotor feedback — i.e., a comparative ranking or selection among candidate architectures, not merely a list of factors affecting embodied performance.

The causal effect of feedback loop properties—specifically sensor feedback latency and reliability—on a language-model-controlled embodied system's capacity for real-time behavioral learning and adaptation, i.e., the mechanism by which delayed or unreliable sensory return degrades or supports online adjustment.

The causal relationship between latency/timing of the sensor-action feedback loop and the system's sensorimotor competence — i.e., the mechanism by which timing characteristics of feedback shape embodied performance.

The causal effect of feedback-loop timing (delay between action and sensed consequence) on a language model's capacity to acquire or refine sensorimotor competence — i.e., the mechanism by which latency helps or degrades learning from embodied experience.

The causal mechanism by which specific embodiment parameters (sensor fidelity and feedback latency) produce divergent behavior in an otherwise identical language model — i.e., how varying each factor changes observed behavior across embodiments.

The causal effect of feedback-loop latency (fast vs. slow feedback cycles) on whether and how qualitatively new embodied capabilities arise, i.e., the mechanism and magnitude by which timing of sensorimotor feedback drives emergence rather than mere incremental performance gain.
The causal mechanisms by which two specific embodiment components—sensor fidelity and the latency/timing of feedback from actions—shape what an embodied language-model system can practically do.

The causal relationship between embodiment parameters (sensor fidelity and feedback latency) and downstream system-level outcomes of reliability and safety, i.e., how varying those parameters changes failure rates and risk profiles across different embodiments of the same language model.

The specific causal relationship between particular embodiment parameters (sensor fidelity, feedback latency) and which categories of tasks an embodied language model can or cannot successfully perform — i.e., a mapping from variation in those parameters to resulting task-capability differences.

The mechanisms by which two specific embodiment components—feedback latency/timing and the surrounding control architecture—shape what an embodied language model can practically do, i.e., the causal pathways linking these system properties to capability differences.
The causal mechanisms by which variation in sensor fidelity and feedback latency shapes a language-model-driven embodied system's capacity to learn and adapt from the consequences of its own actions.

Whether empirical comparison shows that varying the embodiment while holding the language model fixed yields measurably different outcomes (i.e., the existence and detectability of an embodiment effect), not merely the claim that practical capabilities can differ.

An enumeration of the particular practical capabilities that appear, disappear, or are altered for a fixed language model as a function of the specific sensor and actuator configuration it is embodied in.

The causal effect of feedback-loop delay (latency between action and sensed consequence) on a language model's capacity to acquire and refine sensorimotor competence through embodied interaction — i.e., the mechanism by which timing of feedback shapes learning from such interactions.
The mechanism by which specific embodiment properties — feedback latency/timing and the surrounding control architecture — shape what an identical language model can practically do when embodied.

The effect of action-to-feedback latency on a sensor-motor-connected language model's capacity for learning and behavioral adaptation — i.e., how varying feedback delay changes credit assignment and adaptive performance.

The causal effect of feedback delay in an embodied sensorimotor loop on a language model's capacity to acquire or improve competence from that experience — i.e., how varying latency changes learning ability.

A ranking or identification of which embodiment-related factors (e.g., sensor quality, action channels, feedback timing, control architecture) exert the largest influence on an embodied model's practical capabilities.
The causal mechanisms by which feedback latency/timing and control-architecture design shape a language-model-driven embodied system's sensorimotor performance.

The causal mechanism by which the surrounding control architecture (how sensing, action channels, and feedback are organized and mediated around the model) produces or constrains specific practical capabilities in an embodied system, holding the language model fixed.
The causal mechanism by which the latency/timing of sensory feedback relative to actions shapes the behavior and practical capabilities of an embodied language-model system.

Identification of concrete measurement instruments — specific benchmarks, metrics, or evaluation criteria — that would operationalize and quantify the shift from text-mediated competence to sensorimotor competence in an embodied language-model system.

The causal effect of action-feedback delay (latency) on how such an embodied language-model system learns and develops behavior over time — i.e., the mechanism and direction by which faster or slower sensorimotor feedback changes acquired competence and behavioral trajectory.

An enumeration of the specific embodiment-side factors (e.g., sensor quality, action channels, feedback timing, control architecture) and how each constrains or augments a language model's practical capabilities across different physical systems.

The causal effect of action-to-feedback delay on acquisition of sensorimotor competence in an embodied language-model system — i.e., how varying feedback timing changes learning of sensorimotor skills.

The identity and comparative merits of specific control architecture designs for coupling a language model to fast sensorimotor feedback loops — i.e., which architectural arrangements best support such integration.

The causal influence of feedback latency/timing in a sensor-action loop on the quality of a language model's sensorimotor competence — i.e., the mechanism by which timing of consequence-reflecting inputs shapes embodied performance.

The mechanism by which the latency/timing of sensory feedback in an embodied loop shapes what the model can practically do, i.e., the causal influence of feedback timing as one embodiment variable on realized capability.

The specific behavioral or capability changes that arise as sensorimotor coupling becomes richer and faster — i.e., what new or altered capacities appear at increasing levels of integration, not merely that the text/sensorimotor distinction blurs.

The causal effect of feedback-loop latency (delay between action and sensed consequence) on a sensor-actuator-coupled language model's capacity for real-time learning and behavioral adaptation — i.e., the mechanism and direction by which timing delays degrade or constrain online adjustment.

The causal mechanisms and magnitude by which variation in specific embodiment parameters (sensor fidelity, feedback latency) produces differences in task performance for an identical underlying language model.

The specific classes of embodied capability that appear only above some threshold of richness and speed in sensorimotor feedback and control loops, as distinct from capabilities that scale continuously with added sensing and actuation.

The mechanism by which the latency/timing of sensor-action feedback loops shapes what an embodied language-model system can practically do, i.e., the causal role of feedback timing as one embodiment variable determining realized capability.

The causal mechanisms by which embodiment properties (sensor quality, action channels, feedback timing, control architecture) shape what a given language model can practically do, i.e., how variation in these system components changes its effective capabilities.
Evaluation methodology: the criteria, procedures, or benchmarks appropriate for assessing sensorimotor competence in embodied language-model systems, as distinct from text-based evaluation.

A characterization of the specific types or qualities of embodied competence that arise once sensorimotor feedback loops reach sufficient richness and speed — i.e., what new capacities appear beyond incremental information/control gains.

The specific causal mechanisms by which each individual embodiment factor — sensor quality, action channels, and feedback timing — shapes the practical capabilities a language model exhibits in a given embodied system.

The effects of latency between action execution and sensory feedback on the embodied system's behavior and performance — i.e., how increased feedback delay degrades or alters closed-loop control, credit assignment, and competence.

The causal effect of action-to-feedback delay (latency) on a sensorimotor-embodied language model system's learning and adaptation capability — i.e., the mechanism and direction by which varying feedback timing changes credit assignment, adaptation speed, or control quality.
The causal mechanism by which the latency/timing of sensory feedback in an embodied control loop changes what a fixed language model can practically do, holding the model constant across embodiments.

The causal relationship between sensorimotor feedback characteristics (sensor fidelity and feedback latency) and a language-model-controlled embodied system's capacity for real-time learning and behavioral adaptation — i.e., the mechanism and magnitude by which degraded or delayed feedback constrains online adaptation.

The specific causal role of feedback latency/timing between action and sensed consequence in shaping how embodied competence develops in sensor-connected language models — i.e., the mechanism by which timing characteristics affect competence acquisition, as distinct from the general list of factors that influence behavior.

An enumeration of the particular practical capabilities that vary when the same language model is placed in different embodiments (i.e., which specific abilities are gained or lost depending on sensors, action channels, feedback timing, and control architecture).

The causal relationship between properties of the action-consequence feedback loop (its fidelity/quality and timing/responsiveness) and how well the embodied model can use consequences of its own actions to improve or adapt its behavior.

The causal mechanisms by which variation in sensor fidelity and feedback latency within an embodiment changes what a fixed language model can practically do, i.e., how each embodiment factor translates into altered practical capability.

The specific configurations or properties of sensorimotor integration (sensor types, action channels, feedback timing, control architecture) that would mark a qualitative shift from incremental information/control addition to a distinct kind of embodied competence — i.e., the criteria distinguishing that category.
A ranking or identification of which specific types of control architectures (linking model outputs to actuators and sensor feedback) contribute most to producing embodied competence.

An enumeration of the concrete technical difficulties encountered when coupling real-time sensorimotor feedback loops (sensor input, action output, timing, control architecture) to a language model's text-based processing pipeline.

The causal effect of variation in feedback latency across sensorimotor channels on a model's learning and execution of coordinated tasks — i.e., how delay magnitude and mismatch between channels degrade or alter coordination and learning performance.

An enumeration of the concrete technical difficulties encountered when coupling real-time sensorimotor feedback loops to a language model's text-based processing (e.g., latency and timing mismatches, sensor-to-token representation conversion, control-loop stability, action channel grounding).

The location of a threshold — the specific point or criterion along increasing sensorimotor richness and speed at which augmented control becomes genuine embodied competence — including whether any such threshold exists.

A specification of concrete evaluation benchmarks or measurement criteria capable of discriminating text-mediated competence from sensorimotor competence in embodied language-model systems with increasingly rich and fast sensor-action coupling.

The specific types or design features of control architectures linking a language model to sensors and actuators that would yield a qualitatively different kind of embodied competence rather than merely added information and control.
The causal mechanism by which the latency/timing of sensory feedback in an embodied loop shapes what the same language model can practically accomplish.
A causal account of how variation in sensor fidelity and feedback latency changes the dependability of the model's action selection in embodied settings.

Whether the language model's own parameters/internal state are updated by sensorimotor feedback in such embodied systems, versus the model remaining fixed with adaptation occurring only in the surrounding control architecture.
The specific criteria or threshold conditions that would mark the distinction between text-mediated and sensorimotor competence as having become fully blurred rather than merely less tidy.

The mechanisms by which two specific embodiment factors — feedback timing (latency/rate at which action consequences return as inputs) and the surrounding control architecture — shape what a fixed language model can practically do, i.e., how variation in these factors produces differences in practical capability across embodiments.
The causal effect of feedback-loop latency (speed/timing of sensorimotor feedback) on whether and how embodied competence develops in sensor-and-actuator-connected language models.

The identity of specific control architecture designs that are most effective for integrating fast-changing sensorimotor feedback into a language model's action loop — i.e., a comparative ranking/selection among architectural options, not merely a list of factors that matter.

focal_unknown_anchor: As those connections become richer and faster, the boundary between simply adding information and control and producing a qualitatively different form of embodied competence remains unsettled.
